lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of Badr: reasons, events and importance
objectives: Explain why the Prophet fought the Battle of Badr
Describe the main events and outcome
Evaluate the importance of Badr for the establishment of Islam

keywords.def: the first major battle between the Muslims and Quraysh, 17 Ramadan 2 AH
criterion: Badr is called Yawm al-Furqan, the Day of Criterion
a military expedition led personally by the Prophet
payment for the release of prisoners

starter: Define Hijrah and state the year it took place.
Name two groups in Madinah after the Hijrah.
Why was the Qur'an revealed gradually?

teach.heading: Why Badr?
bullets: Muslims had lost homes and property in Makkah
Permission to fight those who wronged them was given (22:39-40)
A Quraysh caravan led by Abu Sufyan travelled near Madinah
The caravan escaped but Quraysh sent an army
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.8b: reasons the Prophet chose to fight. Present the Qur'anic permission 22:39-40 and the context of persecution and confiscated property. Misconception: the Muslims set out to attack a peaceful city; they set out to intercept a caravan and the situation changed (8:7). Ask: what is the difference between defensive and aggressive war?

teach.heading: The battle
bullets: About 313 Muslims against about 1,000 Quraysh
The Prophet prayed through the night for help
Allah promised reinforcement (3:123-125; 8:9)
Muslims won; around 70 Quraysh killed and 70 captured; 14 Muslims martyred
teach.note: State that figures are those commonly reported. Highlight Abu Jahl's death. Ask pupils to calculate the proportion: about 1 Muslim to 3 Quraysh. Link to 33:9 for the pattern of Allah's help in battles (Edexcel passage: 'remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came').

teach.heading: The prisoners
bullets: Prisoners were treated humanely
Most were freed on ransom
Reports mention literate prisoners taught Muslims to read
Allah praises feeding the captive (76:8)
teach.note: Use 'reports state'. The Prophet advised kindness to prisoners (Bukhari: he told Companions to treat them well, per Abu Aziz's narration in the seerah). Compare with ancient norms of killing or enslaving. Ask: what does this show about Islamic ethics in war?

teach.heading: Importance for Islam
bullets: The first great victory increased Muslim confidence
Raised the Muslims' standing among Arab tribes
Showed that faith and trust could overcome numbers
Led Quraysh to seek revenge at Uhud
teach.note: Edexcel 1.8c. Develop 'establishment of Islam': political security for Madinah, morale, and tribal respect. Ask for a counter-argument: was Badr more important than Hudaybiyyah? Prepare for 12-mark.

teach.heading: Exam skill
bullets: Reasons: persecution, confiscation, protection of Madinah
Events: numbers, du'a, help of angels
Result: victory, prisoners, ransom
Importance: morale, status, security
teach.note: Create a four-box planner. Model a 6-mark: 'Explain two reasons why the Battle of Badr was important to the early Muslim community.' Pupils write first reason in PEEL.

practice: Give two reasons why the Muslims fought at Badr.
What does 'Furqan' mean?
Short answer: 'State two ways the prisoners of Badr were treated' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on the importance of Badr.
Create a table of reasons, events, outcome and importance.
Plan a 12-mark answer: 'Badr was the most important battle in the life of the Prophet. Discuss.'
exit: When did Badr take place?
Give one importance of the battle.
lessons.homework: Draft the 12-mark answer; revisit it after Uhud.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: four-box planner with sentence starters; stretch: assess whether Badr was a political, military or religious turning point.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of Uhud: lessons of obedience and patience
objectives: Describe the events of Uhud
Explain why the Muslims initially prevailed and then suffered setbacks
Evaluate the importance of the lessons of Uhud

keywords.def: the battle fought in Shawwal 3 AH near Mount Uhud
the Quraysh cavalry commander at Uhud, later a Muslim general
the Prophet's uncle who was martyred at Uhud

starter: What was the result of Badr?

teach.heading: The build-up
bullets: Quraysh marched with about 3,000 men for revenge
About 700 Muslims went out; 300 hypocrites withdrew
The Prophet placed 50 archers on the hill and ordered them to stay
'Do not leave your position, even if you see us seized by birds' (Bukhari)
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. The consultation: some wanted to meet them outside Madinah; the Prophet agreed to go out. Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with his men. The archer's command is narrated by al-Bara' in Bukhari. Ask: why was the hill vital?

teach.heading: The turning point
bullets: Muslims initially forced the Quraysh back
Many archers left to collect spoils
Khalid ibn al-Walid attacked from behind
A rumour spread that the Prophet had been killed
teach.note: Bukhari narrates that the archers disputed; some remained with Abdullah ibn Jubayr, who was killed. Mus'ab ibn Umayr was martyred, causing the rumour. Qur'an 3:152-153 addresses this: 'Allah fulfilled His promise ... until you lost courage and disputed about the order ...'

teach.heading: Casualties and the Prophet's injuries
bullets: About 70 Muslims martyred including Hamzah and Mus'ab
The Prophet was wounded in the face and lost a tooth
Companions such as Talhah shielded him
Quraysh withdrew but did not capture Madinah
teach.note: From Bukhari and Muslim. Handle with care. Ask: what does his determination to carry on show? Mention the Muslims pursued Quraysh at Hamra al-Asad the next day to show strength (3:172-173).

teach.heading: Lessons from Uhud
bullets: Obedience to the leader is essential
Love of worldly gain can undermine faith
Hardships are tests (3:140-142)
Muhammad is a messenger; Muslims worship Allah, not a man (3:144)
teach.note: Link 3:144 to Abu Bakr's speech at the Prophet's death (a later lesson). Ask: how does losing a battle strengthen faith in the long run? Distinguish between divine promise and human conditions.

teach.heading: Comparison with Badr
bullets: Badr: victory with trust and discipline
Uhud: setback after disobedience
Both teach reliance on Allah and obedience
Both shaped the Muslim community
teach.note: Set up a comparison table. Prepare the 12-mark: 'Uhud was more important than Badr in the development of the early Muslim community. Discuss.' Pupils plan their arguments.

practice: Why were the archers important?
Describe what Khalid ibn al-Walid did.
Short answer: 'State two lessons from Uhud' (2 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Muslims suffered losses at Uhud.'
Create a comparison chart of Badr and Uhud.
Write the opening and conclusion of a 12-mark answer on Uhud's importance.
exit: Who commanded the archers?
Give one lesson of Uhud.
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer using 3:152 or 3:144 as evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: map of the battlefield with arrows; stretch: assess whether disobedience or ambition was the key cause of the setback.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of the Trench (Qur'an 33:9)
objectives: Describe the siege of Madinah and the digging of the trench
Analyse Qur'an 33:9
Explain the importance of the battle

keywords.def: the trench dug to defend Madinah
the Companion who suggested the trench
surrounding a place to cut it off

starter: Give two causes of the Muslims' losses at Uhud.
Why was the Quraysh army at Uhud larger than at Badr?

teach.heading: The threat
bullets: In 5 AH Quraysh and allied tribes formed a confederacy of about 10,000
The Muslims numbered about 3,000
Madinah lacked natural defences on the north
Salman suggested a trench
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.8: the Trench is one of four named battles. Explain the Jewish tribe Banu Nadir's role in rallying the Ahzab after being expelled (4 AH) for plotting against the Prophet. Note this is the seerah account; present factually.

teach.heading: Digging the trench
bullets: The Prophet worked alongside the Companions
They were hungry; some tied stones on their stomachs
A hard rock was struck by the Prophet and broke
Allah gave them hope in hardship
teach.note: Bukhari (Jabir and al-Bara') records the digging, hunger, and the rock. The tying of stones is reported in Tirmidhi and others; Jabir's hadith in Bukhari tells of the small meal that fed many. Ask: how did the Prophet share their hardship?

teach.heading: The siege
bullets: The enemy could not cross the trench
Banu Qurayzah's breach of agreement increased the danger
Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud caused mistrust among the enemy
A bitter storm shattered their camp
teach.note: Qur'an 33:9 (Edexcel passage): 'O you who believe, remember Allah's favour upon you when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see.' Annotate: favour, armies, wind, unseen armies. Treat the Banu Qurayzah aftermath factually: the treaty breach led to a siege and a judgement by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh according to their own law (Bukhari, Muslim). Be prepared to answer questions with sensitivity and sources.

teach.heading: Outcome and importance
bullets: The confederates withdrew
The Prophet said: 'Now we will march against them; they will not march against us' (Bukhari)
Madinah's security was established
Strengthened the Muslims' standing
teach.note: Edexcel 1.8c. Ask: why was this a turning point? Compare 33:9 with Allah's help at Badr. Link to hypocrisy: the hypocrites expressed doubts (33:12-13).

teach.heading: Analysing 33:9
bullets: What does it ask believers to remember?
What did Allah send?
How does it show Allah's power?
What lesson does it give about trust?
teach.note: Model annotation and a 12-mark plan: 'The Battle of the Trench shows that victory comes only through the help of Allah. Discuss.' Include human effort (trench), unity, and divine help.

practice: Why was the trench a good idea?
Identify two parts of Allah's help in 33:9.
Short answer: 'State two details of the siege' (2 marks).
independent: Annotate 33:9 and write three comprehension answers.
Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Battle of the Trench was important.'
Plan the 12-mark answer on divine help and human effort.
exit: Who suggested the trench?
What did Allah send upon the enemy in 33:9?
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer using 33:9 as evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: diagram of Madinah and the trench; stretch: evaluate the role of strategy, morale and divine help.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 The Battle of Khaybar
objectives: Explain the reasons for the expedition to Khaybar
Describe the events and the settlement
Evaluate its importance

keywords.def: a fortified oasis north of Madinah, attacked in 7 AH
the Companion given the flag at Khaybar
tax paid by non-Muslim subjects in return for protection

starter: What did the Prophet say after the Trench?
Name the Companion who suggested the trench.

teach.heading: Background
bullets: After Hudaybiyyah the Muslims turned to the north
Khaybar was a base of tribes hostile to Madinah
Banu Nadir had settled there and helped incite the Ahzab
The Prophet marched in Muharram 7 AH
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.8b: the reasons. Ask pupils to identify the security dimension: removing a threat to Madinah. Mention the numbers: around 1,400-1,600 Muslims. Note that sources differ on small details.

teach.heading: The campaign
bullets: The Muslims besieged the fortresses one by one
Ali was given the flag after the Prophet said: 'I will give the flag to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger'
Ali defeated the champion Marhab
The strongest forts fell
teach.note: The flag hadith is in Bukhari and Muslim (Sahl ibn Sa'd). Ali had sore eyes and the Prophet applied his saliva, and he recovered. Ask: what qualities are praised in the hadith? Avoid exaggerated stories; keep to sources.

teach.heading: The settlement
bullets: The inhabitants surrendered
They were allowed to remain and farm the land
They gave half the produce
The Prophet later sent an assessor to estimate the share
teach.note: From Bukhari and Muslim (Ibn Umar). Ask: why would the Prophet leave them on the land? (They knew farming; the Muslims had few farmers.) Mention that after Khaybar a poisoned meal was offered to the Prophet (Bukhari, Anas); he did not eat from it fully.

teach.heading: Importance of Khaybar
bullets: Removed a northern threat to Madinah
Brought economic resources
Showed Muslim strength after Hudaybiyyah
Prepared the ground for later expansion
teach.note: Edexcel 1.8c. Compare Khaybar with the Trench: from defence to securing borders. Ask: how do you decide which battle was most important? Build criteria: security, morale, economy, spread of Islam.

teach.heading: Evaluating the four battles
bullets: Badr: first victory
Uhud: lessons of obedience
Trench: defence of Madinah
Khaybar: removing a threat
teach.note: Use a ranking diamond. Pupils justify their chosen most important battle. Prepare the 12-mark stem: 'The Battle of Badr was more important than the other battles. Discuss.'

practice: Give two reasons for the expedition to Khaybar.
What arrangement was made after the surrender?
Short answer: 'State two ways Khaybar helped Muslims' (2 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Battle of Khaybar was important.'
Complete a ranking diamond of the four battles with reasons.
Plan the 12-mark answer on the importance of Badr compared with others.
exit: In which year did the expedition to Khaybar take place?
Give one importance of the expedition.
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer comparing Badr with the other battles.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: comparison table with sentence stems; stretch: weigh the importance of military versus political outcomes.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Section A - The battles fought by the Prophet (spec 1.8)
lessons.title: 1.8 Why did the Prophet fight? Rules and ethics of war
objectives: Explain the reasons the Prophet chose to fight
Describe the rules of conduct in war
Evaluate the claim that the battles were defensive

keywords.def: striving in the way of Allah, including self-struggle and, when needed, lawful defence
going beyond the limits set by Allah

starter: Name the four battles in order.
Who was given the flag at Khaybar?

teach.heading: Reasons for fighting
bullets: Persecution and expulsion from Makkah
Self-defence of the community
Protection of allies and treaties
Removal of threats to Madinah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Use 22:39-40 and 2:190. Ask pupils to find each reason in the four battles. Edexcel 1.8b requires explanation, not just listing.

teach.heading: Limits and rules
bullets: 'Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress' (2:190)
Do not kill women, children or the elderly (Bukhari, Muslim)
Do not mutilate or betray
Incline to peace if the enemy inclines to it (8:61)
teach.note: The Prophet forbade killing women and children (Ibn Umar in Bukhari and Muslim). Muslim also reports his instructions to commanders to avoid treachery, mutilation and killing children. Ask: how do these rules compare with modern rules of war?

teach.heading: Treatment of the enemy
bullets: Prisoners were treated well
Agreements were honoured
Forgiveness after victory (Makkah)
Peace treaties such as Hudaybiyyah
teach.note: Link to previous lessons. Ask pupils to give an example for each principle. Misconception: the Prophet fought to force people to accept Islam. Respond with 2:256 ('There is no compulsion in religion').

teach.heading: Evaluating the claim
bullets: Argument for: each was a response to attack or threat
Argument against: Khaybar and later expeditions were pre-emptive
Scholars give security and justice as reasons
Judgement needs evidence
teach.note: Model both sides. Include different viewpoints (Muslim historians and non-Muslim historians). Encourage pupils to use phrases like 'Some argue ... others claim ...'. Provide evidence for each.

teach.heading: Exam practice
bullets: 6 marks: explain two reasons the Prophet chose to fight
12 marks: evaluate whether the battles show the Prophet's concern for justice and peace
teach.note: Plan together; pupils write the 6-mark answer. Remind them to use specific battles and sources.

practice: List three reasons the Prophet fought.
State two rules of conduct from the lesson.
Short answer: 'Explain what 2:190 teaches about fighting' (4 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer: 'Explain two reasons why the Prophet chose to fight battles.'
Plan and draft the 12-mark answer on justice and peace.
Create a poster showing rules of war in Islam with sources.
exit: What does 2:190 say about transgression?
Name one rule of conduct in war.
lessons.homework: Finish the 12-mark answer; include 2:190, 8:61 and an example.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: two-column for/against grid; stretch: analyse differences between modern and classical concepts of just war.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Section A - The final years and achievements (spec 1.9)
lessons.title: 1.9 The final pilgrimage and the Farewell Sermon (Qur'an 5:3)
objectives: Describe the Prophet's final pilgrimage
Outline the main themes of the Farewell Sermon
Analyse Qur'an 5:3

keywords.def: the plain where the sermon was delivered

starter: Name one rule of war from the Prophet.
Which battle was fought in 3 AH?

teach.heading: The last Hajj
bullets: In 10 AH the Prophet led the pilgrimage
A great multitude joined him
He taught the rites: 'Take your rites from me'
He stood at Arafat and delivered his sermon
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Jabir's account is in Sahih Muslim. Explain that this pilgrimage became the model for all later Hajj. Ask: why is it called the Farewell Pilgrimage?

teach.heading: The sermon: sanctity of life and wealth
bullets: Blood and property are sacred
Pre-Islamic blood feuds are abolished
Riba of the days of ignorance is abolished
Everyone is accountable to Allah
teach.note: From Muslim (Jabir). Link to human rights teaching in 1.6. Ask: why does the Prophet emphasise life and wealth first? (Foundation of justice.)

teach.heading: The sermon: equality and women
bullets: All people are from Adam; no Arab over non-Arab except by taqwa
Fear Allah concerning women
Hold fast to the Book of Allah
'Have I conveyed the message?'
teach.note: The Arab/non-Arab wording is in Ahmad (graded authentic). The Prophet ﷺ asked the crowd and they affirmed; he said 'O Allah, bear witness'. Ask: how do these themes support social justice?

teach.heading: Qur'an 5:3
bullets: Prohibited foods are listed
'This day I have perfected your religion for you'
'Completed My favour upon you'
'And approved Islam as your religion'
teach.note: Edexcel 1.9 passage. According to Bukhari, a Jewish man told Umar that if this verse had been revealed to them they would have taken that day as a festival; Umar replied that they knew where and when it was revealed: Arafat on a Friday. Discuss the meaning: the religion's essential teachings were complete.

teach.heading: Exam practice
bullets: 6 marks: explain two themes of the sermon
12 marks: 'The Farewell Sermon is the most important speech in Islamic history. Discuss.'
teach.note: Plan the 12-mark: for (summary of Islam, human rights), against (other sermons or events). Use 5:3 to anchor. Ask pupils to apply their evidence.

practice: List four themes of the Farewell Sermon.
Explain what 'perfected' means in 5:3.
Short answer: 'State two rights mentioned in the sermon' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on two themes of the sermon.
Annotate 5:3 and write a summary.
Plan and write the 12-mark answer.
exit: Where was the sermon delivered?
Quote or paraphrase a line from 5:3.
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer on the Farewell Sermon.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sermon points on cards; stretch: compare the sermon with a modern human-rights document respectfully.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Section A - The final years and achievements (spec 1.9)
lessons.title: 1.9 The Prophet's achievements and his death in Madinah
objectives: Outline the Prophet's achievements in society, religion and politics
Describe the events at his death
Evaluate his greatest achievement

keywords.def: the Highest Companion: his final words in Bukhari
what is left behind after death

starter: Name two themes of the Farewell Sermon.
Which verse says the religion was perfected?

teach.heading: Achievements in religion
bullets: Delivered the Qur'an
Established prayer, zakah, fasting and Hajj
Established Tawhid and ended idol worship in Arabia
Taught moral values and the Sunnah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 1.9c. Ask pupils to list achievements and decide which category they belong in. Remind them of the example of Makkah's idols being removed.

teach.heading: Achievements in society
bullets: Brotherhood of Muhajirun and Ansar
Rights of women, orphans and the poor
Justice and equality before the law
Abolished tribal feuds
teach.note: Link to previous teaching about equality. Give evidence from the sermon and Madinah. Ask: how did the Prophet change the attitude to the weak?

teach.heading: Achievements in politics
bullets: Founded the Madinah community and agreements
Made treaties such as Hudaybiyyah
Sent letters to rulers
United Arabia under Islam
teach.note: Explain that the Prophet corresponded with the leaders of Byzantium, Persia, Abyssinia and Egypt, as in the seerah. Ask pupils to consider leadership qualities.

teach.heading: His death
bullets: He became ill in 11 AH
He asked to be cared for in Aisha's house
Abu Bakr led the prayer during his illness
He died on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH
teach.note: Bukhari narrates that he said 'with the highest companion' (ar-Rafiq al-A'la) before passing, in Aisha's arms. Be sensitive. Ask: what does his final concern for prayer teach? Mention that Abu Bakr was appointed to lead the prayer.

teach.heading: The community's reaction
bullets: Umar could not accept the news at first
Abu Bakr said: 'Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is Ever-Living and never dies'
He recited 3:144
The community chose Abu Bakr as caliph
teach.note: From Bukhari. Ask: how does 3:144 protect Tawhid even after the Prophet? This links to the Tawhid unit. Prepare the 12-mark: 'The Prophet's greatest achievement was in religion, not politics. Discuss.'

practice: Sort achievements into religion, society and politics.
Describe the events at the Prophet's death.
Short answer: 'State two achievements of the Prophet' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer: 'Explain two achievements of the Prophet in society.'
Plan and write the 12-mark answer.
Create a one-page revision sheet for Section A, 1.9.
exit: What did Abu Bakr recite after the Prophet's death?
Give one achievement in each category.
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark answer and revise 1.8-1.9.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sorting cards for achievements; stretch: evaluate how religious, social and political achievements are connected.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Section B - Beliefs: Tawhid and Allah (spec 2.1)
lessons.title: 2.1 The nature of belief in Allah: Tawhid (Qur'an 112:1-4)
objectives: Explain the meaning and importance of Tawhid
Analyse Surah al-Ikhlas
Explain the three categories of Tawhid according to ahl as-sunnah
starter: State what 'Seal of the Prophets' means.

teach.heading: Surah al-Ikhlas
bullets: 'Say: He is Allah, One'
'Allah, the Eternal Refuge'
'He neither begets nor is begotten'
'And there is none comparable to Him'
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 2.1 passage. Annotate each ayah: unity, independence, no parents or children, uniqueness. Also mention the Prophet's statement that it equals a third of the Qur'an (Bukhari).

teach.heading: Meaning and importance
bullets: The foundation of Islam: La ilaha illa Allah
All prophets called to it (21:25)
It shapes worship, trust and character
It is the basis for salvation
teach.note: Ask: if you believe in one Creator, how does that change your relationship with the world? Link to the Sunni understanding of Tawhid as a lived reality, not just a statement.

teach.heading: Three categories
bullets: Rububiyyah: Allah alone is Lord, Creator and Sustainer
Uluhiyyah: Allah alone is worshipped
Asma wa Sifat: Allah's names and attributes are unique and perfect
No likening, no denial
teach.note: This is how ahl as-sunnah classify Tawhid based on the Qur'an and Sunnah. Examples: 39:62 (Rububiyyah), 1:5 (Uluhiyyah), 42:11 (Names and attributes). Pupils produce a chart with example.

teach.heading: Characteristics of Allah in the Qur'an
bullets: Al-Hayy, Al-Qayyum (2:255)
Al-Alim, the All-Knowing
Al-Aziz, Al-Hakim
Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim
teach.note: Edexcel 2.1d. Read Ayat al-Kursi in English. Ask pupils to extract characteristics. Link each to belief and behaviour.

Use 112 to support your explanation
Show how belief in Tawhid affects life

objectives: Explain Allah's omnipotence, creatorship, mercy and justice
Use Qur'anic evidence to support explanations
Evaluate how the attributes balance each other

keywords.def: the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

starter: List the three categories of Tawhid.

teach.heading: Omnipotence
bullets: 'Allah is over all things Competent' (2:20)
'Be, and it is' (36:82)
Nothing is beyond His power
Belief inspires trust and humility
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: how does belief in an All-Powerful Creator change fear and hope? Explain tawakkul. Edexcel 2.1b: omnipotence.

teach.heading: Creator
bullets: Allah created the heavens, earth and humans
'Allah is Creator of all things' (39:62)
Creation shows His wisdom and power (3:190)
We are accountable as His servants
teach.note: Ask pupils for examples of signs of creation. Connect to gratitude and responsibility as khalifah. Note that creation implies ownership and care.

teach.heading: Merciful
bullets: 'My mercy encompasses all things' (7:156)
Prophet: 'My mercy overcomes My anger' (Bukhari, Muslim)
Every surah but one begins with bismillah
Hope and repentance
teach.note: Mention the hadith of the mother and child (Bukhari, Muslim), in which the Prophet said Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child. Ask: how does mercy motivate good deeds?

teach.heading: Just
bullets: 'Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight' (4:40)
Every deed is weighed (21:47)
Justice requires accountability
Allah's justice and mercy work together
teach.note: Discuss how mercy and justice balance: hope and fear. Misconception: justice means no mercy. Correct with the hadith that Allah's mercy has a hundred parts (Muslim). Prepare the 12-mark stem: 'Allah's mercy is more important than His justice. Discuss.'

teach.heading: Putting attributes into practice
bullets: Trust Allah in difficulty
Be merciful and just to others
Seek forgiveness
Worship with love and fear
teach.note: Pupils plan how each attribute affects behaviour. Exam link: use specific attributes with examples from the Qur'an.

Explain how mercy and justice complement each other.

Give one effect belief in His mercy has.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Section B - Beliefs: Tawhid and Allah (spec 2.1)
lessons.title: 2.1 Shirk and nifaq (hypocrisy)
objectives: Define shirk and nifaq
Explain why they are condemned
Analyse examples and consequences

keywords.def: hypocrisy: outwardly showing faith while hiding disbelief or insincerity

teach.heading: Shirk
bullets: 'Allah does not forgive that partners be set up with Him' (4:48)
'Shirk is a great injustice' (31:13)
Greatest sin: making a rival to Allah (Bukhari, Muslim)
Includes idols, worship of the self, and giving Allah's rights to others
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain 4:48: Allah does not forgive dying upon shirk, but forgives less for whom He wills; repentance before death is accepted. Edexcel 2.1c. Examples: idolatry; asking the dead to remove harm. Pupils define major and minor.

teach.heading: Minor shirk and riya
bullets: Showing off in worship
Seeking praise from people
Swearing by other than Allah
Reliance on omens
teach.note: Scholars consider these minor shirk and grave sins; riya can nullify the reward of a deed. Link to the hadith of intentions. Ask: how can a teenager guard against riya on social media?

teach.heading: Nifaq: hypocrisy
bullets: The munafiqun professed faith but hid disbelief (63:1-3)
'The hypocrites are in the lowest depths of the Fire' (4:145)
Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew at Uhud
Nifaq in deeds: lying, breaking promises, betraying trust
teach.note: Distinguish major nifaq (belief) from minor (actions). Hadith: three signs of the hypocrite (Bukhari, Muslim). Remind pupils that only Allah knows hearts and we do not accuse individuals.

teach.heading: Consequences
bullets: Loss of reward in the Hereafter
Division and harm to the community
Spiritual emptiness
Repentance is always open (4:146)
teach.note: Highlight the exception in 4:146: those who repent, reform and hold fast to Allah. Ask: how does Islam combine warnings with hope?

teach.heading: Exam link
bullets: Explain what shirk and nifaq mean
Give Qur'anic evidence
Explain why each is condemned
teach.note: Model a 6-mark: 'Explain two reasons why shirk is the greatest sin in Islam.' Plan the 12-mark: 'Nifaq is as dangerous to the Muslim community as shirk. Discuss.'

Give examples of major and minor shirk.

independent: Write the 6-mark answer on why shirk is the greatest sin.

Create a table comparing shirk and nifaq.
exit: Give a verse that condemns shirk.
Name one sign of hypocrisy.

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Section B - Prophethood and revelation (spec 2.2-2.3)
lessons.title: 2.2 Risalah: the importance of prophethood and the earlier prophets (Qur'an 9:128-129)
objectives: Explain the nature and importance of prophethood
Describe the lives of Adam, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Musa, Dawud and Isa
Analyse Qur'an 9:128-129

keywords.def: protection of prophets from major sins and errors in conveying the message
a miracle given to a prophet by Allah's permission

teach.heading: What is prophethood?
bullets: Prophets are chosen men who receive revelation
They convey Allah's message and show how to live
'We sent to every nation a messenger' (16:36)
They are human, not divine (18:110)
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 2.2a-b. Ask: why do humans need guidance? Emphasise that prophets are role models. Include belief in all prophets without distinction (2:285).

teach.heading: Adam, Ibrahim and Isma'il
bullets: Adam: first human and prophet; repented (2:37)
Ibrahim: stood for Tawhid; tested with the idols and sacrifice
Isma'il: patient son; helped build the Ka'bah
Hajj rites recall Ibrahim and family
teach.note: Keep to Qur'anic and sound accounts. Ibrahim's rejection of idols: 21:51-70; his test: 37:102-107; building of the Ka'bah: 2:127. Ask: how is Hajj linked to Ibrahim?

teach.heading: Musa, Dawud and Isa
bullets: Musa: led Bani Isra'il from Pharaoh; received the Tawrah
Dawud: king and prophet; received the Zabur
Isa: born miraculously to Maryam; received the Injil
Isa is a messenger of Allah, not divine (4:171)
teach.note: Be respectful toward Christians and Jews: Muslims honour Musa and Isa as prophets. Explain differences in belief clearly and politely. Ask: what does the Qur'an say about Isa's miracles by Allah's permission (3:49)?

teach.heading: Qur'an 9:128-129
bullets: 'There has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves'
'Grievous to him is what you suffer'
'Eager for you; to the believers kind and merciful'
'Sufficient for me is Allah; on Him I rely'
teach.note: Edexcel passage. Annotate: closeness, compassion, trust. Link to the Prophet's care for his ummah (hadith: du'a 'my Ummah, my Ummah' in Muslim). Ask: what qualities of a prophet appear?

teach.heading: Importance and lessons
bullets: Prophets deliver guidance and show how to apply it
They teach patience, trust and mercy
They unify humanity under one message
Muhammad is their seal
teach.note: Prepare 6-mark: 'Explain two lessons Muslims learn from the lives of the prophets.' Pupils choose two prophets. 12-mark stem: 'The prophets are more important as role models than as messengers. Discuss.'

practice: Match each prophet to a key event or book.
State two qualities of prophets.
Short answer: 'Explain why prophets were sent' (4 marks).
independent: Write a 6-mark answer using two prophets as examples.
Annotate 9:128-129.
Plan the 12-mark answer on prophets as role models.
exit: Name two prophets and their books.
Give one quality of the Prophet Muhammad from 9:128.
lessons.homework: Write the 12-mark answer on role models.

lessons.title: 2.3 The holy books of Islam (Qur'an 4:163)
objectives: Describe the nature of the Tawrah, Zabur, Injil and Scrolls of Ibrahim
Explain the importance of the holy books in establishing Islam
Analyse Qur'an 4:163

keywords.def: guardian and criterion over earlier scriptures (5:48)

starter: Name three prophets from the previous lesson.
Which verse says there is a messenger to every nation?

teach.heading: Revelation through books
bullets: Books are Allah's words given to messengers
The message was the same: worship Allah alone
The Qur'an is the final revelation
Belief in the books is a pillar of iman
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 2.3. Link to the hadith of Jibril. Ask: why did Allah send books as well as prophets?

teach.heading: Qur'an 4:163
bullets: 'We have revealed to you as We revealed to Nuh and the prophets after him'
Lists Ibrahim, Isma'il, Is'haq, Ya'qub, Isa and others
'And We gave Dawud the Zabur'
One chain of revelation
teach.note: Edexcel passage. Annotate names. Ask: what does the verse show about the unity of revelation?

teach.heading: Earlier books
bullets: Suhuf of Ibrahim
Tawrah to Musa
Zabur to Dawud
Injil to Isa
teach.note: Explain Muslim belief that these were true revelations. Muslims believe that the Qur'an corrects and confirms what is true (5:48) and that earlier texts changed over time, a view that Muslims hold respectfully. Avoid disparaging language. Ask: what does it mean for the Qur'an to be a criterion over earlier books?

teach.heading: The importance of the books
bullets: Show that Allah guides every nation
Establish Tawhid and the Day of Judgment
The Qur'an completes and confirms earlier guidance
Muslims respect the earlier prophets and their books
teach.note: Edexcel 2.3b. Pupils suggest how respect for earlier books leads to respectful relations with Jews and Christians (People of the Book, 29:46: 'do not argue except in the best way'). Ask: how can this guide interfaith conversations?

teach.heading: Exam link
bullets: Name each book and prophet
Explain the role of the Qur'an as final
Link to belief in prophets
teach.note: Model a 6-mark: 'Explain two reasons why Muslims believe in the earlier holy books.' 12-mark: 'The Qur'an is the only holy book Muslims need. Discuss.' Plan together and balance points on respect for earlier books and the Qur'an's finality.

practice: Match each prophet with their book.
Explain what 'muhaymin' means.
Short answer: 'State two reasons Muslims believe in earlier books' (2 marks).
independent: Write the 6-mark answer on belief in earlier holy books.
Annotate 4:163 with the list of prophets.
Plan and write the 12-mark answer on the Qur'an as the only book needed.
exit: Name the four earlier books or scrolls.
What does 5:48 say about the Qur'an?

lessons.bigQuestion: What do the lives of the earlier prophets teach Muslims about faith, patience and leadership?
objectives: Describe the main events in the lives of six earlier prophets as the Qur'an presents them
Explain what each prophet's role teaches Muslims
Use the stories as evidence in an exam answer

Most: explain one lesson from three prophets
Some: assess how far the prophets share one message

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patience and trust in Allah ﷻ; Moral: learning from the examples of the prophets

keywords.def: the friend of Allah (khalil Allah), who built the Ka'bah
prophet who received the Tawrat and confronted Pharaoh
prophet and king who received the Zabur
the Messiah, born of Maryam, who received the Injil

starter: What is the difference between a nabi and a rasul?
Which ayah is the set passage for risalah?

teach.heading: One message, many prophets
bullets: All prophets called to worship Allah ﷻ alone
They were human, chosen and protected
Muslims believe in all of them without distinction (Qur'an 2:285)
The Qur'an mentions 25 by name
teach.note: Bismillah. This lesson deepens the Y11 unit 2.2 lesson with more detail on each prophet. 2:285 states belief in all messengers, making no distinction; verify. Make it clear that Muslims love and honour all prophets and say 'peace be upon him' after each name. Ask pupils which prophets they already know.

head: Prophet
Key events in the Qur'an
Lesson
rows: Created, honoured by angels, tested, forgiven
Rejected idols, tested with sacrifice, built the Ka'bah
Obedient son; helped build the Ka'bah
Confronted Pharaoh, led Bani Isra'il, received the Tawrat
King and prophet, Zabur, defeated Jalut
Born miraculously, spoke in the cradle, gave Injil

teach.heading: Adam, Ibrahim and Isma'il
bullets: Adam: created from clay; Allah ﷻ taught him the names; he repented (Qur'an 2:30-37)
Ibrahim: rejected idols (Qur'an 21:51-70) and was tested
Ibrahim's dream of sacrificing his son (Qur'an 37:102-107)
Ibrahim and Isma'il raised the Ka'bah (Qur'an 2:127)
teach.note: Check ayat references: 2:30-37 (Adam), 21:51-70 (Ibrahim and idols), 37:102-107 (the sacrifice), 2:127 (building the Ka'bah). Verify wording in the mushaf. Note that the Qur'an does not name the son in 37:102-107; most scholars say Isma'il (and some said Ishaq); say 'the majority of scholars hold it was Isma'il'. Present neutrally.

teach.heading: Musa, Dawud and Isa
bullets: Musa: Pharaoh's court, the Exodus, Tawrat
Dawud: Jalut defeated; Zabur; king with justice
Isa: birth (Qur'an 19:16-33), miracles by Allah's permission
Isa is not divine; Qur'an 5:75 calls him a messenger
teach.note: Musa is the most-named prophet in the Qur'an (mention without a number unless verified). Dawud: 2:251 (defeating Jalut); 38:17-26 (Dawud). Isa: 19:16-33 and 3:45-49; 5:75 'The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger'. Verify all. Teach respectfully for Christian and Jewish classmates; do not mock other beliefs. Muslims believe Isa will return before the Day of Judgment: a Muslim belief held by many and described in hadith; teacher to supply references if needed.

bullets: Facts
Lessons
Link
teach.note: Model a 6-mark answer.

model.problem: Explain what the life of Ibrahim teaches Muslims. (6 marks)
steps: Point: Ibrahim rejected idol worship, showing that belief in one Allah ﷻ must be held even when the community disagrees.
Explain: Muslims learn to stand for Tawhid.
Point: he was ready to sacrifice his son at Allah's command, and Allah ﷻ replaced the sacrifice (37:102-107).
Explain: this teaches ultimate obedience and trust, remembered every year at Eid-ul-Adha and Hajj.

lessons.unit: Spec 2.4: al-Qadr (Section B)
lessons.title: 2.4 al-Qadr: the nature of predestination and free will
lessons.bigQuestion: If Allah ﷻ knows everything, are humans really free?
objectives: Explain the Muslim belief in al-Qadr
Explain how al-Qadr and free will fit together
Link to accountability on the Day of Judgment
successCriteria: All: define al-Qadr and free will
Most: explain how Muslims reconcile qadr and responsibility
Some: assess views of how qadr and free will relate
lessons.crossCurricular: Philosophy and Ethics: free will and determinism; Science: cause and effect
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: trust (tawakkul); Moral: personal responsibility

keywords.def: Allah's knowledge and decree of all things
relying on Allah while taking action

starter: Name the six pillars of iman.

teach.heading: Belief in al-Qadr
bullets: Allah ﷻ knows everything before it happens
Allah ﷻ wrote it in a preserved record (Qur'an 57:22)
Everything created has a measure (Qur'an 54:49)
One of the six articles of faith (Muslim 8)
teach.note: Bismillah. Muslim 8 is the hadith of Jibril that lists iman including qadr, its good and evil. Teacher to verify the wording. 57:22 and 54:49 are secure; verify. Explain: Allah's knowledge encompasses time; it does not mean humans are forced.

teach.heading: Free will and responsibility
bullets: Qur'an 18:29: let whoever wills believe or disbelieve
Humans choose within what Allah ﷻ has allowed
Reward and punishment depend on choice
Hadith: act, for each is eased to what he was created for (Bukhari 4949, Muslim 2647)
teach.note: 18:29 secure; verify. Hadith 'Work, for everyone is eased to that for which he was created' (Bukhari 4949; verify). Ask: why would the Companions still act? They did. Two simple analogies: a teacher knows a student will fail without forcing it. Scholars discuss positions such as human 'acquisition' (kasb) of acts that Allah ﷻ creates; for exam level, present the common view: Allah's knowledge does not remove human choice. Neutral note: some early groups denied qadr or denied human choice; most Muslims reject both extremes.

left.title: Allah's knowledge and will
points: Allah knows all and wills what exists

right.title: Human choice
points: People choose between right and wrong and are accountable

teach.heading: Qur'an 92:5-10 and the hadith on predestination
bullets: Those who give, fear Allah ﷻ and believe in the best: ease
Those who are stingy and think they need no help: hardship
Hadith: 'everyone is eased to that for which he was created'
Link: effort and trust together
teach.note: The spec uses a hadith and 92:5-10; teacher should read the printed passage. 92:5-10 refers to 'al-husna' meaning belief in the best (Paradise or the truth). Teach: the ayat show consequences follow choices. Do not allow fatalism; the Prophet ﷺ taught effort. Hadith: 'The strong believer is better than the weak...do not say if only' (Muslim 2664; verify).

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Explain
Connect
Illustrate
teach.note: Model a 6-mark answer.

model.problem: Explain how Muslims believe al-Qadr and free will are connected. (6 marks)
steps: Point: Muslims believe Allah ﷻ knows everything that will happen, written in a record (57:22).
Explain: but knowing is not forcing; humans still choose.
Point: 18:29 says whoever wills may believe or disbelieve.
Explain: so on the Day of Judgment people are judged for what they chose, which only makes sense if they are responsible.

Allah does not know the future
check.why: Muslims hold both Allah's knowledge and human responsibility.

lessons.title: 2.4 al-Qadr: the early community, and the nature of evil and suffering
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a good Allah ﷻ allow suffering?
objectives: Explain the significance of al-Qadr for the early Muslim community
Explain Muslim teaching about the nature of evil and suffering
Evaluate responses to the problem of suffering
successCriteria: All: give two Muslim responses to suffering
Most: explain how belief in qadr helped the early Muslims
Some: assess whether Muslim explanations of suffering are convincing
lessons.crossCurricular: Philosophy and Ethics: the problem of evil; PSHE: resilience and bereavement
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patience (sabr) and gratitude; Moral: helping those who suffer

teach.heading: Qadr and the early community
bullets: Faith in qadr gave courage in battle and hardship
Companions accepted loss with patience
They acted and trusted: tying the camel and trusting Allah ﷻ
Umar and the plague: from Allah's decree to Allah's decree (Bukhari 5729, Muslim 2219)
teach.note: Teach the principle: belief gave strength and perspective, not passivity. The plague story: Umar turned back from Sargh (verify). Quotation: 'Flee from Allah's decree to Allah's decree' attributed to Umar in this report. Link to Y10 unit 1.4 on Hijrah hardship.

teach.heading: Evil and suffering in Islam
bullets: Life is a test (Qur'an 67:2 and 2:155)
Allah ﷻ does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (Qur'an 2:286)
Suffering can expiate sins (Bukhari 5641, Muslim 2573)
The believer's affair is all good: patience and gratitude (Muslim 2999)
teach.note: Verify all ayat and hadith numbers. 2:155-156 'We will surely test you with fear, hunger...': secure. Distinguish natural suffering (disease, earthquakes) from human evil (oppression): the second comes from misuse of free will and Allah ﷻ demands justice for it. Be sensitive: pupils may be bereaved or have personal experience; do not use suffering as a debate point, and offer pastoral support (safeguarding).

teach.heading: Evaluating answers
bullets: Strength: gives meaning and hope
Strength: explains accountability for human evil
Challenge: why so much suffering for the innocent?
Muslim reply: life is short; the Akhirah is the full answer
teach.note: Encourage pupils to evaluate fairly: Muslim teaching gives meaning, but critics ask about children and animals. Responses: the world is a place of testing; Allah's wisdom exceeds ours; compensation in the Hereafter; 2:216 'you may dislike something that is good for you'. Verify 2:216 before quoting.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: For
Against
Judgement
teach.note: Model a 12-mark plan.

model.problem: 'The existence of suffering shows that Allah ﷻ does not care.' Assess this statement. (12 marks)
steps: For: critics say innocent suffering seems unfair.
Muslim view: life is a test; Allah ﷻ is Most Merciful and Just; justice will be completed on the Day of Judgment.
Muslim view: patience brings reward; suffering can expiate sins (Bukhari 5641).
Judgement: Muslims reject the statement, relying on Allah's mercy and the Akhirah, but accept that suffering is painful and demands compassion.
model.answer: Level 4: balanced arguments and a reasoned conclusion.

check.q: What is the Muslim view of human evil, such as oppression?
options: It results from human choices, and Allah will judge it
check.why: It results from misuse of free will and will be judged.

Define sabr.
What did Umar say about the plague?

Mubah: neutral

keywords.def: successor: leader of the Muslim community

starter: Where did the Prophet ﷺ die?
Who supported him at the cave?

teach.heading: After the Prophet's death
bullets: Death in 11 AH; Umar's disbelief, Abu Bakr's calm
Abu Bakr recited 3:144 and said Muhammad ﷺ had died but Allah ﷻ lives (Bukhari 3667)
The community chose Abu Bakr at Saqifah
Qur'an 9:117: Allah ﷻ turned to the Prophet ﷺ, Muhajirun and Ansar
teach.note: SENSITIVE and neutral: Sunni Muslims hold that the community chose Abu Bakr by consultation and the Prophet's indications (he led prayers in his illness); Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet ﷺ designated Ali (referring to Ghadir Khumm) and that leadership belonged to Ali and the Imams. Teach the position of Ahl al-Sunnah as the Academy's belief and describe other views accurately and respectfully because the specification requires it; do not argue or mock. 3:144 secure; verify. 9:117 is the set passage. Check before use: Abu Bakr recited 3:144 and said Muhammad ﷺ had died but Allah ﷻ lives (Bukhari 3667; verify)

teach.heading: Abu Bakr (11-13 AH)
bullets: Faced those who refused zakah and false prophets
Sent the army of Usamah
Collected the Qur'an (Zayd ibn Thabit)
Began the campaigns into Syria and Iraq
teach.note: Teach: Ridda wars; unity; Qur'an compilation (link to 1.2); first expeditions. His first address: 'Obey me as long as I obey Allah ﷻ': widely quoted from early sources; teacher to check the wording and source before using. Keep dates approximate.

teach.heading: Umar ibn al-Khattab (13-23 AH)
bullets: Conquered Syria, Iraq, Egypt, Persia
Set up the diwan, courts and Hijri calendar
Famous for justice and humility
Assassinated in 23 AH while leading prayer
teach.note: Teach: Jerusalem accepted a treaty (the covenant to the people of Aelia); the Hijri calendar from the Hijrah; Umar's simplicity. Avoid unverified anecdotes: teacher should verify any story before telling it. Link to the importance of consultation (shura).

keywords.def: a written copy of the Qur'an

teach.heading: Uthman (23-35 AH)
bullets: Standardised the written Qur'an and sent copies
Expanded to North Africa, Cyprus, and farther east
Known for modesty and generosity
Unrest led to his assassination in 35 AH
teach.note: Link to unit 1.2. Neutral note: criticism of Uthman's governors and the revolt is discussed in history; Sunni sources honour him as a rightly-guided caliph; Shia sources differ on his rule. Teach accurately and calmly: his murder by rebels is a sad event in Muslim history. Avoid taking sides in modern disputes.

teach.heading: Ali (35-40 AH)
bullets: Cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ; chosen after Uthman
Faced civil conflicts at Camel and Siffin
Known for knowledge, courage and justice
Killed in 40 AH by a Kharijite
teach.note: Neutral note: Sunni Muslims count Ali as the fourth rightly-guided caliph; Shia Muslims regard him as the first Imam and rightful successor. Both honour his knowledge and piety. Explain that the conflicts were about justice for Uthman's killers and authority; do not assign blame to Companions. Keep the tone respectful. Teach the position of Ahl al-Sunnah as the Academy's belief and describe other views accurately and respectfully because the specification requires it; do not argue or mock. Safeguarding: avoid sectarian jokes or disrespect in class and remind pupils of the school's respectful conduct.

teach.heading: Why the period matters
bullets: It preserved the Qur'an and Sunnah
It spread Islam and set up government and law
It gave models of consultation and justice
It also shows the dangers of division
teach.note: Hadith: 'Hold fast to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly-guided caliphs' is reported in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi; verify before quoting. Ask: what lessons can leaders today take from this period?

For: law, courts and government were developed.
Against: later centuries brought great scholarship and civilisations.
Judgement: it was the foundation for everything after it, so it can be argued to be the most important.

lessons.title: 3.6 Jihad: meaning, origins, and the greater and lesser jihad
lessons.bigQuestion: What does jihad mean, and what is the greater jihad?
objectives: Define jihad and describe its origins
Explain the difference between greater and lesser jihad
Explain the importance of the greater jihad in daily Muslim life
successCriteria: All: define jihad and give one example
Most: explain the greater and lesser jihad accurately
Some: assess why the inner struggle is central to Muslim life
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: self-discipline; Citizenship: law of the land, peaceful action

keywords.def: striving or struggle for Allah's sake

starter: Who was the Prophet's first wife?

teach.heading: What does jihad mean?
bullets: Arabic root: to strive, to struggle
Not 'holy war': the word means effort
Many forms: self, family, society, knowledge, defence
Qur'an 29:69: those who strive for Us, We will guide
teach.note: SENSITIVE: the word is often misused in the media and by extremists. Teach carefully; reassure pupils that mainstream Muslim teaching rejects terrorism, and safeguarding means any pupil expressing extremist views is referred to the DSL under the school's safeguarding procedures. 29:69 secure; verify. Ask: where do you hear the word jihad? What does it mean in Arabic? Bismillah. Check before use: A word of truth to an unjust ruler (Abu Dawud 4344; verify)

teach.heading: Greater and lesser jihad
bullets: Greater jihad: struggle against own desires and wrongdoing
Lesser jihad: outward struggle, including defending the community
Hadith: the strong one controls himself in anger (Bukhari 6114, Muslim 2609)
A hadith about 'returning from the lesser to greater jihad' is not considered reliable
teach.note: Important teacher knowledge: the saying 'we have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad' is widely quoted but scholars such as Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Hajar graded it as not authentic; do not present it as an authentic hadith. The idea of striving against the self is supported by other sources, for example Qur'an 29:69 and Hadith about the mujahid who strives against his own self (Tirmidhi 1621; verify). Neutral note: some Muslim traditions (including many Sufi and Shia scholars) use the greater/lesser terminology freely; spec requires it.

teach.heading: Forms of jihad in daily life
bullets: Struggle to pray on time and be honest
Care for parents (Bukhari 3004, Muslim 2549)
A word of truth to an unjust ruler (Abu Dawud 4344)
Seeking knowledge and serving the community
teach.note: Bukhari 3004: a man asked to join jihad; the Prophet ﷺ asked about his parents and said strive in them; verify. Link to Surah 25:52, 'strive against them with the Qur'an a great striving' (Makkan: striving by argument). Ask: which is harder, controlling anger or fighting? Pupils write examples.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Meaning
Types
Importance
teach.note: Model an exam answer.

model.problem: Explain the difference between the greater and lesser jihad. (6 marks)
steps: Point: the greater jihad is the inner struggle against sin and selfishness.
Explain: it happens daily, in prayer, honesty and patience.
Point: the lesser jihad is outward struggle, such as defending the community when attacked, with strict rules.
Explain: because the lesser jihad has conditions and is rare, the greater jihad is considered the constant duty.

lessons.title: 3.6 The conditions and limits of lesser jihad (Qur'an 2:190-194 and 22:39)
lessons.bigQuestion: When, if ever, is fighting permitted in Islam, and what limits apply?
objectives: Explain the conditions for lesser jihad in the Qur'an
Describe rules of conduct in war
Explain why individuals and groups may not declare jihad, and the role of the law of the land
successCriteria: All: state three limits on fighting
Most: explain 2:190-194 and 22:39 with context
Some: assess how Islamic teaching on conditions answers extremist claims
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: law, terrorism and the rule of law in the UK; History: just war ideas
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice, restraint and mercy; Social: responsibility to the law of the land

keywords.def: the recognised ruler who may declare defensive war
covenant of security: protection for those in a treaty

starter: Which hadith is not considered reliable?

teach.heading: Qur'an 22:39 and 2:190-194
bullets: 22:39: permission to those who are fought, because they were wronged
2:190: fight in Allah's way those who fight you, but do not transgress
2:193: fight until persecution ends
2:194: retaliation is limited to equal
teach.note: These are the passages named in the spec; verify translation in the mushaf. Context: Madinah, after persecution, expulsion, and attack; 22:39 is traditionally considered among the earliest permission to fight. Highlight the repeated command not to transgress (la ta'tadu). Ask: what does 'those who fight you' tell us? Stress defence and restraint. Teacher should keep the discussion rooted in text and history. Check before use: No mutilation or destruction of crops and houses of worship; widely reported in the instructions of Abu Bakr (teacher to verify source)

teach.heading: Rules of conduct
bullets: No killing of women, children and non-combatants (Bukhari 3014, Muslim 1744)
No mutilation or destruction of crops and houses of worship; widely reported in the instructions of Abu Bakr
Honour treaties; keep promises
Qur'an 2:256 and 5:32: no compulsion; sanctity of life
teach.note: Verify the numbers: the prohibition on killing women and children is in Bukhari 3014 and Muslim 1744. The ten commands of Abu Bakr are cited in the Muwatta and Bayhaqi; their chain is discussed, so use as 'reported guidance' only. Mention 5:32. Ask: how do these compare with modern ideas on conduct in war?

head: Allowed
Limited by
rows: Do not transgress; stop when the enemy stops
Declared by legitimate authority, not individuals
Justice and peace, not conquest of belief

teach.heading: Who decides? The law of the land
bullets: Defensive war is for a legitimate authority, not individuals
Terrorism and attacks on civilians are forbidden
Muslims in Britain live under a covenant of security and must keep the law
Whoever kills a person with a covenant will not smell Paradise (Bukhari 3166)
teach.note: FLAG for safeguarding: be clear that nobody has permission to declare jihad on their own, that violence against civilians is haram, and that Muslims in Britain are bound by the law and by the covenant of security. Bukhari 3166: verify. Invite questions respectfully; if a pupil expresses sympathy with extremist ideas, follow the school's safeguarding procedures. Do not run an open debate on current conflicts.

For: rules such as no killing of non-combatants and honouring treaties apply.
Against: some argue that any violence is wrong; many Muslims emphasise peace and the greater jihad.
Judgement: the teaching accepts defence only, with strict limits, which cannot justify terrorism or acts by individuals.

starter: What is the month of Hajj?

teach.heading: Eid-ul-Fitr
bullets: 1 Shawwal: the end of Ramadan
Zakat al-Fitr paid before the prayer
Eid prayer, new clothes, gifts, visiting family
Gratitude for completing the fast
teach.note: Bismillah. Eid-ul-Fitr: no fasting on that day. The hadith about the Eids: the Prophet ﷺ said Allah ﷻ replaced the two days of play with two better days (Abu Dawud 1134, Nasa'i 1556; teacher to verify). Zakat al-Fitr purifies the fasting and feeds the poor. Ask: how is it connected to the end of Ramadan?

teach.heading: Eid-ul-Adha
bullets: 10 Dhul-Hijjah, after Arafah
Remembers Ibrahim's obedience (Qur'an 37:102-107)
Animal sacrificed and shared in three parts
Qur'an 22:37: it is taqwa that reaches Allah ﷻ
teach.note: Verify 37:102-107 and 22:37. The sharing in thirds (family, relatives and friends, poor) is common practice; scholars encourage but do not fix; verify. Link to Hajj. Safeguarding: be sensitive to animal welfare; explain that Islam requires humane treatment and the sacrifice is a religious ritual for those who can afford it.

teach.heading: Meaning and values
bullets: Gratitude
Generosity and charity
Obedience and trust in Allah ﷻ
Family and community
teach.note: Ask pupils to compare using the table. Highlight the idea that both Eids come after acts of worship: fasting and Hajj. Discuss how Muslims in Britain celebrate: prayers in parks, halls, mosques; school holiday requests.

Explain: Muslims learn obedience and trust.
Point: the sacrifice is shared with family and the poor.
Explain: it teaches generosity and community, the aim being taqwa (22:37).

keywords.def: the first month of the Islamic calendar

starter: What month starts the Hijri year?

teach.heading: Origins: Musa and Pharaoh
bullets: 10 Muharram: Allah ﷻ saved Musa and his people from Pharaoh
The Prophet found the Jews of Madinah fasting and said Muslims have more right to Musa
He fasted and urged fasting (Bukhari 2004, Muslim 1130)
Fasting the 9th or 10th is encouraged
teach.note: Verify the numbers. Many Sunni scholars recommend fasting the 9th and 10th (or the 10th and 11th). Frame respectfully; the day is shared with the story of Musa that pupils know from 2.2. Ask: why did the Prophet ﷺ fast on it? (Gratitude to Allah ﷻ for saving a prophet.)

teach.heading: Origins: Karbala
bullets: Husayn, grandson of the Prophet ﷺ, refused to give allegiance to Yazid
He and his family and companions were killed at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH
Shia Muslims commemorate with mourning gatherings, recitation and processions
Sunni Muslims honour Husayn and grieve the tragedy with patience
teach.note: SENSITIVE: present factually and respectfully; do not argue about rival interpretations. Shia Muslims observe the first ten days of Muharram with majalis (gatherings), recitation, charity and food; some communities hold processions. Practices such as self-harming mourning are debated even among Shia scholars; avoid graphic detail, safeguarding age-appropriate. Many Sunni scholars hold that mourning rituals beyond sorrow and patience are not part of the Sunnah; teach the Sunnah of Ashura (fasting, with gratitude to Allah) as the Academy's practice, and describe other communities' practice factually for the exam.

right.title: Common Shia practice
points: fasting on the day is not the usual practice

teach.heading: Meaning for Muslims
bullets: Gratitude and trust in Allah's help
Standing for truth and justice, even at great cost
Patience in hardship
Unity: shared love for the Prophet's family
teach.note: Ask: what can Muslims of all traditions learn from Ashura? Stress sensitivity for pupils from families who observe it. Safeguarding: avoid putting individual pupils on the spot about their family's practice.

Explain: this makes it a day of gratitude and trust in Allah ﷻ.
Point: for many Muslims it remembers the death of Husayn at Karbala.

starter: Name one right of women taught by the Prophet ﷺ.

teach.heading: Qur'an 30:21
bullets: Among His signs: He created mates from yourselves
So you may find tranquillity in them
He placed between you affection and mercy
In that are signs for people who reflect
teach.note: 30:21 وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَنْ خَلَقَ لَكُم مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا لِّتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا وَجَعَلَ بَيْنَكُم مَّوَدَّةً وَرَحْمَةً. Teacher to verify. Ask: what three qualities are named? (Tranquillity, mawaddah, rahmah.) Marriage is described as a sign of Allah ﷻ and a source of peace. Hadith to the young men: marry if you can afford, otherwise fast (Bukhari 5066, Muslim 1400; verify).

teach.heading: Teachings about marriage
bullets: Marriage is encouraged (Qur'an 24:32)
Both parties must consent (Bukhari 5136, Muslim 1419)
The groom gives mahr to the bride (Qur'an 4:4)
Witnesses, announcement and a walimah
teach.note: SENSITIVE: safeguarding and law. In the UK a person must be 18 to marry, and forced marriage is a crime; the Islamic teaching requires consent and Muslims in Britain must also follow UK law, including registering a legal marriage. A nikah alone may not be a legal marriage in England and Wales; encourage a civil registration. Be clear that forced marriage is against Islamic teaching and the law. If any pupil raises concerns, follow safeguarding procedures. Verify hadith numbers and 24:32, 4:4. Note: polygyny is permitted in 4:3 with conditions; the spec does not require it; scholars discuss it and UK law prohibits it; mention only if asked, briefly.

teach.heading: Purposes of marriage

Protecting chastity and modesty
Raising children and building the ummah
Mutual support and kindness (Qur'an 4:19)
teach.note: Discuss how marriage supports individuals and society. Note: the Prophet ﷺ said the best are those best to their wives (Tirmidhi 3895, Ibn Majah 1977; verify). Ask pupils how the three qualities of 30:21 look in practice.

hook.text: If Allah is One, what follows for how a Muslim lives every day?

Hypocrites in the lowest depth of the Fire (4:145)

check.q: Which is an example of nifaq?

teach.heading: Risalah (2.2): set passage 9:128-129
bullets: A Messenger from among yourselves (9:128)
Grieved by your suffering; kind and merciful
'Sufficient for me is Allah' (9:129)
Earlier prophets: Adam, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Musa, Dawud, Isa
teach.note: Risalah is needed because humans need guidance from Allah on how to worship and live. The messengers are examples and warners. Portal lesson y11 13 covers the earlier prophets' lives.

practice.q: Explain what 112:1-4 teaches about the nature of Allah.
practice.a: He is One, the Eternal Refuge on whom all depend, not born and has no child, and nothing is like Him: so He alone deserves worship.

independent.model: Teacher models the first sentence of each: 'Shirk is regarded as the greatest sin because it gives to others what belongs to Allah alone ...' and 'Risalah matters because Allah sent messengers from among people, as 9:128 says ...'

independent.q: Extend: give one way belief in each attribute (omnipotent, creator, merciful, just) affects a Muslim.
independent.a: Trust; gratitude; hope and repentance; fairness and accountability.

starter.a: He lies, breaks promises, betrays trust

starter.q: Which ayah says shirk is unforgiven if unrepented?

teach.heading: 2.3 The holy books
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Portal lessons y11 12, 14 and 15 are independent study. The Qur'an is final and protected (15:9) and confirms and guards over earlier books (5:48).

teach.heading: 2.4 Set passage: the hadith and 92:5-10
bullets: Every person's place is already written
'Shall we not rely on that and stop acting?'
'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for'
Then he recited 92:5-10
teach.note: Narrated by Ali (Bukhari and Muslim). 92:5-10: whoever gives, fears Allah and believes in the best reward, We will ease him towards ease; whoever is stingy, thinks himself free of need and denies the best, We will ease him towards difficulty. Knowledge is Allah's; action and choice are ours.

teach.heading: Decree and free will
teach.note: Early debates: some groups denied qadar (the Qadariyyah); others denied human choice (the Jabriyyah). Sunni scholars hold both: Allah's complete decree and real human responsibility. Shia theology also affirms qadar and especially stresses Allah's justice ('adl) and human free will.

teach.heading: Evil and suffering
bullets: Life is a test (67:2)
Patience in loss: 'To Allah we belong' (2:155-156)
Much evil comes from human choices
Justice is complete in the Akhirah
teach.note: 12-mark statement for 2.4: 'If everything is decreed, people cannot be held responsible for their actions.' Assess this statement.

check.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ answer to 'shall we just rely on what is written?'
options: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for'
check.why: He commanded action: decree does not cancel responsibility. Saying nothing is written denies qadar.

practice.q: Explain what the hadith on predestination and 92:5-10 teach about al-Qadr.
practice.a: Allah knows and has written everyone's end, yet people must act; each is eased towards what they choose: giving and taqwa lead to ease, stinginess and denial to difficulty.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: the hadith teaches that Allah has already written each person's destination. Evidence: ... Explain: but the Prophet ﷺ said "act", so knowledge does not remove choice. Then 92:5-10 shows ...'

practice.q: Which ayah says life is a test of who is best in deeds?

independent.q: 12-mark answer in the portal response box (or Forms long answer): 'If everything is decreed, people cannot be held responsible for their actions.' Assess this statement.
independent.a: For: if Allah wrote everything, choice seems unreal; Jabriyyah view. Against: the hadith 'act'; 92:5-10; 99:7-8; Allah's justice; Shia emphasis on free will. Weighing and justified conclusion.
independent.model: Teacher models the 'for' opening: 'Some people argue that if Allah has decreed everything, humans are not truly free. For example, the hadith says every person's place is already written ...'

independent.q: Extend: explain why Muslims believe the earlier books are not in their original form.
independent.a: They were entrusted to their communities and changed over time (2:79); only the Qur'an is promised protection (15:9).

exit.q: Which book was given to Dawud (4:163)?
Back to our ponder: why do actions matter if Allah knows the end?
exit.a: His knowledge does not force us; we choose and are judged; 'act'.

lessons.bigQuestion: How would you live differently if you were certain your deeds would be weighed?
objectives: To understand Muslim belief about life after death and about the angels
successCriteria: All: describe the stages of the Akhirah
Most: explain the set passages 101:1-11 and 2:97-98
Some: explain how belief in the Akhirah and angels affects Muslim life
lessons.smsc: Moral: accountability for our actions

keywords.def: the barrier between death and resurrection

hook.text: How would you live differently if you were certain your deeds would be weighed?
hook.a: Muslims believe exactly this (101:6-9): heavy scales bring a pleasing life; light scales bring the Fire.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasing life. But as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be an abyss' (al-Qari'ah 101:6-9).

starter.q: Which book was given to Isa?
What did the Prophet ﷺ answer about relying on what is written?
starter.a: 'Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for'

starter.q: Which surah follows the predestination hadith?
Which ayah says life is a test?

teach.heading: 2.5 Stages of the Akhirah
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Portal lessons y11 16, 17 and 34 are independent study. Barzakh: 23:100.

timeline.label: Death
timeline.text: The soul is taken by the Angel of Death (32:11)

timeline.label: Barzakh
timeline.text: The life of the grave until resurrection (23:100)

timeline.label: Resurrection
timeline.text: All are raised; the Horn is blown (39:68)

teach.heading: Set passage: 101:1-11
bullets: The Striking Calamity: what is it? (101:1-3)
People like scattered moths; mountains like wool (101:4-5)
Heavy scales: a pleasing life (101:6-7)
Light scales: the abyss, a blazing Fire (101:8-11)
teach.note: Annotate the imagery: moths show confusion and weakness; carded wool shows the power of that Day. Link to Allah's justice (2.1).

teach.heading: 2.6 Malaikah: set passage 2:97-98
bullets: Jibril brought the Qur'an to the heart of the Prophet ﷺ
Enmity to Jibril and Mika'il is enmity to Allah
Angels are created from light and always obey (66:6)
teach.note: Portal lesson y11 18 is independent study. Roles: Jibril, revelation; Mika'il, provision and rain (as scholars explain); Israfil, the Horn (named in hadith); the Angel of Death (malak al-mawt, 32:11; the name Izra'il is used by many Muslims but is not in the Qur'an).

check.q: Which angel is named with Jibril in the set passage 2:97-98?
check.why: 2:98 names Jibril and Mika'il. Israfil is named in hadith; Malik in 43:77; the Angel of Death in 32:11.

teach.heading: Effect on Muslim life
bullets: Accountability: every deed weighed
Hope: Allah's mercy and Jannah
Angels record deeds: honesty in private
Patience: justice is complete in the Akhirah
teach.note: Pupils need 'explain how belief affects' answers for both topics.

practice.q: Explain how belief in the Akhirah affects the way Muslims live.
practice.a: They know deeds will be weighed (101:6-9), so they do good and avoid wrong; they hope for Jannah and fear Jahannam; they bear hardship knowing justice comes.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: belief in the Akhirah makes Muslims careful about their actions. Evidence: 101:6-9 says those whose scales are heavy will have a pleasing life. Explain: so Muslims try to add good deeds and avoid sin. Link: belief shapes behaviour daily.'

practice.q: What is the Barzakh?
practice.a: The barrier between death and resurrection
options: The barrier between death and resurrection

independent.q: Two set-passage answers in the portal response box: a) 'Explain what 101:1-11 teaches about the Day of Judgement.' b) 'Explain what 2:97-98 teaches about the angels.'
independent.a: a) A shocking Day, scales of deeds, outcomes of heavy and light scales. b) Jibril brings revelation by Allah's permission; angels are honoured servants; enmity to them is enmity to Allah.
independent.model: Teacher models the opening of a): 'Qur'an 101:1-11 describes the Day of Judgement as al-Qari'ah, the Striking Calamity, which shows ...'

independent.q: Extend: name the roles of four principal angels.
independent.a: Jibril revelation; Mika'il provision; Israfil the Horn; the Angel of Death takes souls.

exit.q: What happens to those whose scales are heavy (101:6-7)?
Back to our ponder: how would you live differently?
exit.a: More careful, honest and generous, knowing every deed is weighed.

lessons.title: Fast-teach 2.7 to 2.9: Shari'ah, Islamic etiquette and the early leaders (Qur'an 5:48, 49:11-13, 9:117)
lessons.bigQuestion: Does a society need laws? Where should good laws and good manners come from?
objectives: To understand the Shari'ah and its sources, Islamic etiquette, and the importance of the early leaders
successCriteria: All: name the four sources of Shari'ah and the five categories
Most: explain the set passages 5:48 and 49:11-13
Some: explain Sunni and Shia views of the early leaders with 9:117

keywords.def: the way and law given by Allah
analogy: applying a ruling to a similar new case
a successor; a caliph leading the community

hook.text: Does a society need laws? Where should good laws and good manners come from?
hook.a: Muslims believe the best guidance comes from Allah: the Shari'ah, and adab taught in the Qur'an and Sunnah.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'To each of you We prescribed a law and a clear way' (al-Ma'idah 5:48), and 'The most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you' (al-Hujurat 49:13).

starter.q: Which two angels are named in 2:97-98?

starter.a: The barrier between death and resurrection

starter.q: Which surah describes the Striking Calamity?

teach.heading: 2.7 Shari'ah: sources and categories
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Portal lessons y11 19 to 24 are independent study. Sunni sources: Qur'an, Sunnah, ijma', qiyas. Twelver Shia scholars use the Qur'an, the Sunnah (including the Imams' teachings), ijma' and 'aql (reason) in place of qiyas. Qiyas example: drugs are forbidden by analogy with intoxicating drink.

teach.heading: 2.8 Set passage: 49:11-13
bullets: Do not mock others or use offensive nicknames (49:11)
Avoid suspicion, spying and backbiting (49:12)
Humanity from one pair, made nations to know one another (49:13)
Most noble: the most righteous
teach.note: Portal lessons y11 21 and 22 cover adab with speech and eating (bismillah, right hand, eat from what is in front of you: Bukhari and Muslim).

teach.heading: 2.9 The early leaders: set passage 9:117
bullets: Allah forgave the Prophet ﷺ, Muhajirun and Ansar
They followed him in the hour of hardship
Sunni: four Rightly Guided Caliphs in order
Shia: Ali appointed as first Imam
teach.note: 9:117 refers to the expedition of Tabuk. Sunni: Abu Bakr (632 to 634), Umar (634 to 644), Uthman (644 to 656), Ali (656 to 661). Shia Muslims believe the Prophet ﷺ appointed Ali as leader (citing Ghadir Khumm) and follow a line of Imams. Teach factually; portal lessons y11 23 and 24 are independent study.

check.q: Which is a source of Shari'ah meaning 'agreement of scholars'?
check.why: Ijma' is consensus. Qiyas is analogy; adab is manners; mubah is a category of action.

teach.heading: Why it matters
bullets: Shari'ah guides all of life, not only courts
Adab builds trust and unity
The early leaders: models of sacrifice and justice
teach.note: 12-mark statement for 2.7: 'A society needs laws, and the Shari'ah gives Muslims the guidance they need.' Assess this statement.

practice.q: Explain what 49:11-13 teaches Muslims about how to treat others.
practice.a: Do not mock or insult; avoid suspicion, spying and backbiting; all humans are equal in origin and the most noble is the most righteous, so no racism or pride.
practice.model: I do: 'Point: 49:11 forbids mocking others. Explain: those mocked may be better than those mocking, so pride is wrong. Point: 49:13 teaches that humans were made into nations to know one another. Explain: ...'

practice.q: Which category is 'disliked'?
practice.a: Makruh

independent.q: Table then paragraph (portal response box): complete the five categories with your own examples; then 'Explain the importance of the early leaders for Muslims', using 9:117 and both Sunni and Shia views.
independent.a: Correct categories and examples. Paragraph: they kept Islam united after the Prophet ﷺ, spread it, compiled the Qur'an; 9:117 praises the Muhajirun and Ansar; Sunni and Shia views stated fairly.
independent.model: Teacher models one row ('Fard: obligatory; example: fasting Ramadan') and the paragraph's opening sentence.

independent.q: Extend: explain how qiyas works with an example.
independent.a: A new case shares the reason ('illah) of an old ruling, so the ruling applies: drugs intoxicate like alcohol, so they are haram.

exit.q: Who was the second caliph for Sunni Muslims?
Back to our ponder: where should good laws and manners come from?
exit.a: For Muslims: Allah's guidance in the Qur'an and Sunnah, applied by scholars.
